name: Lavender

soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Lavender loves sandy, gritty soil that drains fast.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: loam or shallow rocky soil with good drainage
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Loam or shallow rocky soil is fine, as long as it drains well.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: heavy or wet clay that holds water around the roots
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy or wet clay is a problem because it holds water around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Lavender is a Mediterranean sub-shrub that does best in poor, dry ground with very little organic matter; rich, moist soil produces soft, floppy growth and invites root rot. Amend heavy clay for drainage before planting rather than adding fertility.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Lavender likes poor, dry, gritty soil and full sun. That sounds backward, but it comes from the dry Mediterranean hills, so rich, damp soil actually makes it weak and rot-prone. If your soil is heavy clay, mix in coarse material so water drains fast, and skip the compost.

ph.note_seasoned: Lavender prefers a near-neutral to slightly alkaline soil, roughly pH 6.5 to 7.5, and tolerates alkaline ground up to about 8.0. In acidic soils a light addition of garden lime brings the pH up. This alkaline tolerance is part of why it suits dry-climate and high-pH gardens.
ph.note_beginner: Lavender likes soil that is neutral to a little bit chalky (about pH 6.5 to 7.5, and it copes up to around 8.0). If your soil is on the acidic side, a small amount of garden lime nudges it where lavender wants it.

tip_seasoned: Treat lavender mean: full sun, lean fast-draining soil, deep but infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and rich soil are the top killers, not cold. Shear it back by about a third after bloom every year, cutting into green growth only and never into the bare woody base.
tip_beginner: The trick with lavender is to not fuss over it. Give it the sunniest, driest, best-draining spot you have, water it deeply but only once in a while, and do not feed it much. After it finishes blooming, trim about a third off the leafy green growth (never down into the hard woody stems) so it stays bushy instead of going leggy.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Lavender has very low fertility needs and is one of the few plants you can harm by feeding. A single inch of compost worked in at planting, or one application of a slow-release fertilizer for the season, is plenty. Over-fertilized plants put on lush foliage at the expense of flowers and fragrance and become more prone to disease and winter injury.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Lavender barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer actually hurts it. A little compost mixed in when you plant is enough. Feed it heavily and you get a big leafy plant with few flowers that is more likely to get sick or die back in winter.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: N/A. Lavender is not fed by N-P-K targets; a lean soil and minimal-to-no supplemental feed is the goal, so no fertilizer analysis applies.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: N/A. There is no fertilizer number to hit here, since the aim is to feed lavender as little as possible.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most 1 inch of compost at planting, or one slow-release application per season.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

companions.note_seasoned: Lavender pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water plants that share its lean, dry, sharply drained conditions; group it with drought-tolerant perennials rather than thirsty, rich-soil neighbors. As a strong pollinator draw it also supports nearby flowering plants. Avoid siting it among plants that need frequent water, which forces conditions that rot lavender.
companions.note_beginner: Plant lavender next to other plants that also like full sun and dry soil, such as drought-tolerant perennials. Keep it away from plants that need a lot of water, because the wet soil those plants want will rot your lavender.

good_seasoned.name: Echinacea (coneflower)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A drought-tolerant perennial that shares lavender's full-sun, low-water conditions and extends the pollinator season; listed by extension among plants commonly grown with English lavender.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Echinacea is a drought-tolerant, full-sun, lean-soil prairie perennial whose cultural needs closely match lavender's, so the pairing is sound co-cultivation: one waterwise bed suits both and avoids the overwatering that rots lavender, plus both are strong pollinator draws with contrasting form (coneflower disks vs lavender spikes). traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility + pollinator benefit, horticulturally well-supported but not a measured pest/yield effect.

good_seasoned.name: Salvia
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A sun-loving, low-water perennial with similar lean-soil needs, commonly paired with lavender in extension guidance.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Ornamental salvias share lavender's full-sun / well-drained / low-water requirements (many are close relatives of culinary sage), and their flower spikes echo lavender's form while extending the bloom season. Co-cultivation compatibility + pollinator draw. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.name: Rudbeckia (black-eyed Susan)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shares lavender's drought tolerance and full-sun siting; listed by extension as a common lavender companion.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Rudbeckia is a tough, drought-tolerant, full-sun native perennial tolerant of poor soil, matching lavender's conditions; golden daisies contrast lavender's purple and both draw pollinators. Co-cultivation + pollinator. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.name: Gaillardia (blanket flower)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A heat- and drought-tolerant perennial suited to the same lean, dry soil, named by extension among low-water plants grown with lavender.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Gaillardia is a heat- and drought-tolerant, full-sun, lean-soil perennial squarely in lavender's cultural range, with long warm-season bloom and strong pollinator appeal. Co-cultivation + pollinator. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.name: Daylily
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A tough, low-maintenance perennial that tolerates dry conditions and is listed by extension as a common lavender companion.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Daylily is a tough, low-maintenance full-sun perennial often paired with lavender for structure and contrast. Caveat lowering confidence: daylilies tolerate (and arguably prefer) richer, more moisture-retentive soil than lavender's lean, dry, sharply-drained ideal, so the cultural match is looser than the Mediterranean-herb/prairie-perennial companions. traditional/low: a common, attractive pairing but with a real soil/water-preference mismatch, so flagged at low confidence.

good_seasoned.name: Iris
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Shares lavender's preference for good drainage and full sun; listed by extension among plants commonly grown with English lavender.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bearded iris in particular shares lavender's love of full sun and sharp drainage (rhizomes rot in wet soil, like lavender crowns), making it a sound dry-border companion with strong vertical/structural contrast and early-season bloom that extends interest before lavender peaks. Co-cultivation compatibility. traditional/medium (assumes bearded/dry-loving iris; moisture-loving iris types e.g. Siberian/Japanese would be a poor match).

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Echinacea (coneflower)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot and brings in pollinators.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same shared-conditions co-cultivation + pollinator basis as the good_seasoned Echinacea entry. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Echinacea is one of the most reliable lavender partners because it asks for the same things: full sun, lean soil, and not much water. That shared appetite is the real reason it works, you can run the whole bed on a waterwise schedule without the overwatering that rots lavender at the crown. The broad, flat coneflower heads also play off lavender's narrow spikes, and the two bloom together as a pollinator draw. Site them in the same free-draining ground and resist the urge to pamper either.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Salvia
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Another sun-and-dry-soil plant that grows happily next to lavender.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Salvia. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Salvia and lavender are natural bedfellows, many ornamental salvias are cousins of culinary sage and want the identical conditions: full sun, sharp drainage, low water. Growing them together means one easy, dry-loving border rather than a watering compromise. The salvia's flower spikes echo lavender's shape while often blooming longer into the season, and both keep the bees busy. Plant in the same lean, well-drained soil and water sparingly once established.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rudbeckia (black-eyed Susan)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Tough and drought-tolerant, so it shares lavender's conditions.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Rudbeckia. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Rudbeckia is a tough prairie native that thrives on the same neglect lavender does, full sun, poor-to-average soil, and minimal water once it is going. That makes it an easy companion that will not pull the bed toward the rich, damp conditions lavender hates. Its golden, dark-eyed daisies are a bold contrast to lavender's purple haze, and both feed pollinators through summer. Keep the soil lean and well-drained for both.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Daylily
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Easygoing and handles dry soil well alongside lavender.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Daylily, including the soil/water-preference mismatch caveat. traditional/low.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Daylilies are nearly indestructible and add bold strappy foliage and big blooms next to lavender's fine texture, which is why the pairing is popular. One honest caveat for the seasoned eye: daylilies are happy in richer, moister soil than lavender's lean, dry, sharply-drained ideal, so site them at the edge of the dry border rather than in the heart of it, and water to the lavender's tune (sparingly) so you do not push the lavender toward crown rot. A handsome combination as long as you manage to lavender's drier standard.

pests.name: Spittlebug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in late spring, with the small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established lavender plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Blobs of white froth that look like spit on the stems in late spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs, which shelter inside their own foam while feeding on plant sap. Numbers are usually low and the damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.cause_beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly. No treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No specific prevention is warranted. Keeping plants spaced for airflow and not overwatering keeps lavender vigorous enough to shrug off minor pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Nothing special is needed. Giving plants room and not overwatering keeps lavender healthy enough to handle small pests.

pests.name: Whiteflies and aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional clusters of tiny white flies or soft aphids on new growth, most likely on stressed or overcrowded plants in poor conditions rather than on healthy lavender.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, tiny white flies or small soft bugs on new growth, usually only on plants that are stressed or too crowded.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find lavender. Lavender has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that sometimes show up. Lavender has very few pest problems and rarely needs spraying.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers climb. Removing nearby stressors and improving airflow usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Giving the plant more air and removing stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, and good spacing, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed lavender rarely attracts these pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep lavender in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy plants rarely get these bugs.

diseases.name: Phytophthora root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed crown at the soil line. It is the disease of concern for lavender and is tied to wet conditions and poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main disease that kills lavender, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Water mold pathogens that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Wet feet, not cold, is the underlying cause.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let lavender sit in wet ground. On clay, use a mound or raised bed, and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let lavender sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small spots or blotches on the foliage, more likely in humid weather or on crowded, poorly ventilated plants. It is a minor issue compared with root and crown rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small spots on the leaves, more likely in damp weather or on crowded plants. It is a minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi favored by damp, still air around the plant. Crowding and overhead watering raise the risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: Leaf fungi that like damp, still air around the plant. Crowding and watering from above make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected foliage, improve airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. The annual cut-back also helps clear and renew the canopy.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off the spotted leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. The yearly trim helps too.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants at least 2 to 3 feet apart for air circulation, site in full sun, and avoid overhead watering. Good airflow is the main defense.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Leave 2 to 3 feet between plants for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. Good air movement is the main thing.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. After planting, water about once a week until established; mature plants need roughly half a gallon every two weeks until flower buds form, then once or twice a week through bloom and harvest.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not often. A new plant wants about a soak a week until it settles in; an established lavender needs only a little water every couple of weeks, with a bit more while it is flowering.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 gallon per plant per week while establishing; roughly 1/2 gallon every two weeks once mature, until bud formation.
watering.amount_beginner: Roughly a gallon a week for a new plant, then much less once it is established.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Avoid wetting the foliage and crown, which invites root and crown rot.
watering.method_beginner: Pour water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Wet leaves and a soggy crown are what make lavender rot.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting or dieback of whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite regular watering signal too-wet roots and likely Phytophthora root or crown rot, not drought.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If leaves yellow and shoots wilt or die back even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water, not too little. Soggy roots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Established lavender rarely shows true drought stress; brief wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to increase watering.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Lavender almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that bounces back by morning is fine.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 gallon per plant per week
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters: water a new lavender about once a week, roughly a gallon per plant, until it is established. Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings, keeping the foliage and crown dry against Phytophthora root and crown rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water a new lavender about a soak a week until it settles in, roughly a gallon a plant. Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings, keeping the crown dry.

schedule_by_stage.rate: roughly 1/2 gallon every two weeks; a bit more through bloom
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once established, taper off sharply: a mature lavender needs only about half a gallon every two weeks until flower buds form, then once or twice a week through bloom and harvest. The single most common way to kill lavender is overwatering, so when in doubt, water less and let the soil dry well between waterings.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Once established, cut way back: a mature lavender needs only a little water every couple of weeks, with a bit more while it is flowering. More lavender dies from too much water than too little, so when in doubt, water less.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through dormancy an established lavender wants next to no water; wet winter soil around the crown is the classic killer, so ensure sharp drainage and do not let a dormant plant sit wet.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter an established lavender needs almost no water. Soggy winter soil rots the crown, so make sure it drains well and never sits wet.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The single most common way to kill lavender is overwatering. When in doubt, water less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Remember: more lavender dies from too much water than too little.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters; taper off sharply once the plant is established.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water fairly regularly the first year while it gets established, then back off a lot.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Nursery transplants are already hardened; set them out after the last spring frost. If you start from cuttings, harden the rooted plants gradually before planting out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you buy a plant from a nursery, you can put it straight in the ground after your last spring frost. There is no seed-starting step to worry about.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Lavender is almost always started from a nursery transplant or from softwood cuttings taken after bloom, not from seed. English lavender does not come true from seed and germination is slow and variable (roughly 100 to 200 days from seeding to a plantable size), so named cultivars are propagated vegetatively. To raise it from seed anyway, cold-stratify the seed for three to six weeks (moist, in the refrigerator) to improve and even germination, then surface-sow at about 70°F since light aids germination, starting indoors roughly 10 weeks before the last frost; expect slow, erratic emergence.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy and reliable way to grow lavender is to buy a small plant, or take a cutting from an existing one. Growing it from seed is slow and unpredictable, and seed-grown plants often do not match the parent, so most gardeners skip it. If you do want to grow it from seed, chill the seed in the refrigerator for a few weeks first, then surface-sow it and do not cover it, since it needs light to sprout; keep it around 70°F, start indoors about 10 weeks before your last frost, and be patient, because it comes up slowly and unevenly.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering; lavender must never sit in standing water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A gritty, fast-draining potting mix, not a moisture-retaining one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in coarse sand or perlite so water runs straight through.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A coarse, free-draining potting medium; avoid peat-heavy moisture-retentive mixes.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add coarse sand, perlite, or fine gravel to sharpen drainage.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check the soil, but still let it dry between waterings and never leave the pot in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container lavender needs only a very light feed, if any; do not over-fertilize.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In cold-winter areas, or with tender Spanish or French lavender, grow it in a pot you can move into an unheated but protected spot for winter, then bring it back out in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Where the chosen species is not reliably hardy, a container lets you overwinter the plant under cover (an unheated garage or porch); keep it on the dry side and protected from hard freezes, then return it outdoors after frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Lavender grows well in containers, which is the standard way to keep tender Spanish or French types and to grow lavender in the coldest zones where it is treated as a bring-in plant. Use a wide, free-draining pot, re-pot into fresh gritty mix each spring, and never let it stand in water.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Lavender does fine in a pot, which is handy if your winters are very cold or you are growing one of the tender types. Use a wide pot with holes in the bottom and a gritty mix, and tip out any water that collects in the saucer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers keep the medium too consistently moist for lavender and promote root rot; use a conventional free-draining pot instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for lavender; they keep the soil too wet and the roots rot.

recommended.name: Munstead
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9.
recommended.note: Compact English lavender, sweet fragrance, good for cooking and borders.

recommended.name: Hidcote
recommended.hardiness_note: Hardy, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9.
recommended.note: Deep violet-blue English lavender, strong sweet scent, compact; a kitchen favorite.

recommended.name: Phenomenal
recommended.hardiness_note: Vigorous and nearly as hardy as English lavender; bushy compact habit.
recommended.note: Large lavandin hybrid, excellent for drying and fragrance, blooms once in summer.

recommended.name: Grosso
recommended.hardiness_note: Vigorous lavandin, slightly less cold-hardy than English; large plant.
recommended.note: Classic long-stemmed lavandin for crafts, wands, and oil; one summer bloom.

recommended.name: Spanish lavender
recommended.hardiness_note: Tender, hardy only to about zone 7 to 8; grow in a container to overwinter indoors in colder zones.
recommended.note: Showy pineapple-shaped blooms with petal-like bracts; ornamental only, not for cooking.

recommended.name: French lavender
recommended.hardiness_note: Tender, hardy only to about zone 8; a bring-in container plant in colder regions.
recommended.note: Toothed gray-green foliage, long bloom in mild climates; ornamental, not culinary.

varieties.note_seasoned: Lavender reaches the grower as four practical groups on one plant page. English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, e.g. Munstead and Hidcote) is the hardiest and the type used in cooking. Lavandins (L. x intermedia, e.g. Grosso and Phenomenal) are larger, vigorous hybrids best for drying and oil and nearly as hardy. Spanish (L. stoechas) and French (L. dentata) lavenders are tender, showy, ornamental-only types grown in pots and overwintered indoors where winters are cold. Pick English if you want one hardy plant for both the garden and the kitchen.
varieties.note_beginner: There are a few kinds of lavender. English lavender (like Munstead or Hidcote) is the toughest and the one you cook with, so it is the best all-rounder. The big hybrid types (lavandins like Grosso) are great for drying and scent. The frilly Spanish and French types are pretty but not cold-hardy and are mainly for looks, grown in pots in cold areas. If you want just one plant, choose an English lavender.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: N/A as fresh produce storage. Fresh-cut stems last about a week in water as a bouquet; the main keeping method for lavender is drying, not refrigeration.
storage.room_temp_beginner: N/A. Lavender is not stored like a vegetable. Fresh stems last about a week in a vase; otherwise you dry it.
storage.fridge_seasoned: N/A. Lavender is not kept in the refrigerator for storage; cut stems are either used fresh or dried.
storage.fridge_beginner: N/A. You do not store lavender in the fridge.
storage.freezer_seasoned: N/A. Lavender is dried for long-term keeping rather than frozen.
storage.freezer_beginner: N/A. Lavender is dried, not frozen, to keep it.
storage.notes_seasoned: To dry lavender, cut stems as the first buds open, gather them into small bundles of 50 to 100 stems secured with a rubber band, and hang them upside down in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place. Once dry, strip the buds and store them in a sealed, opaque container away from light and air, which fade the color and scent.
storage.notes_beginner: Dry lavender by tying the stems in small bunches and hanging them upside down somewhere cool, dark, and airy. When they are dry, you can leave them as bundles or rub the buds off into a sealed jar kept out of the light, so they hold their color and smell.

rotation.note_seasoned: N/A. Lavender is a long-lived perennial that stays in place for a decade or more, so annual crop rotation does not apply. When replanting an old lavender bed, choose a fresh, well-drained site to avoid carrying over soil-borne root rot.
rotation.note_beginner: N/A. Lavender is not rotated like a vegetable because it is a permanent plant that stays put for years. If you replace an old one, pick a fresh, well-draining spot.

growth_stages.name: Plant out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set the nursery plant out after the last spring frost, in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot you have. Space plants 18 to 24 inches apart, and on heavy ground plant on a mound or raised bed rather than digging sand into clay.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After your last spring frost, plant the small lavender you bought in the sunniest, best-draining spot. Leave about 18 to 24 inches between plants so each one has room and good airflow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A compact young plant with silvery foliage and firm roots filling the nursery pot, ready to set out once frost has passed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small bushy plant with silver-green leaves and roots that hold the potting soil together when you slide it out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen the rootball, set the crown level with the soil surface, and water in once to settle the roots. Do not amend with rich compost or fertilizer; lavender wants lean ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Gently loosen the roots, plant so the top of the rootball is level with the soil, and water once to settle it. Skip the fertilizer and rich compost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: type or cultivar, number set out, and the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down which lavender you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year one)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. Lavender spends year one building roots rather than putting on a full show, and reaches full size in about three years.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. Your lavender is busy growing roots, not making a big display yet, and will not reach full size for about three years.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new silvery growth and the first flower spikes. Light flowering is fine, but the plant should be shaping up bushy rather than stretching.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: New silvery leaves filling in and maybe a few flower spikes. You want it growing bushy and round, not tall and leggy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper toward deep, infrequent watering. Pinch or lightly clip early flowers and shape the plant to encourage bushy lateral growth. Hold off on fertilizer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water fairly often until the plant takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Pinch off the first few flowers and lightly shape it so it grows bushy. Do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: planting-out date, watering taper, and any early shaping.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you planted it and that you are watering less as it settles.

growth_stages.name: Spring leaf-out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Each spring the plant pushes fresh green growth from the base and lower stems. This is the growth you cut into, never the bare wood below it.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Every spring, new green growth appears low on the plant. This soft green growth is the part you trim later, not the hard woody stems beneath it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New soft green shoots emerging along the lower stems and crown, signaling the plant has come through winter and is growing again.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Soft green shoots coming out low on the plant in spring. That tells you it survived winter and is growing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: If you held a hard cut for spring, make it now once green growth has emerged and frost has passed, cutting into green only. Begin deep, infrequent watering as the soil warms.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: If you waited until spring to trim, do it now that you can see green growth and frost is over, cutting only into the green. Start watering deeply but not often.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Spring leaf-out: date green growth appeared and any spring pruning done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when spring growth started and if you trimmed.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The summer flowering window and the time to cut for use. English types often flower late spring into early summer and may rebloom; lavandins bloom once, later in summer.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Summer, when lavender flowers and when you cut it to use. The English kinds often bloom in late spring to early summer; some types flower later.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower spikes coloring up on tall stems. For fresh fragrance and the best dried color, harvest as the lowest flowers on each spike begin to open.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Purple flower spikes on tall stems. For the best scent and dried color, cut them as the bottom flowers on each spike are just starting to open.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut flower stems for use as the spikes begin to open. Keep watering deep and infrequent, and do not feed; over-watering and rich soil reduce both flowering and fragrance.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Cut flower stems as they start to open. Keep watering deeply but rarely, and do not fertilize, since too much water or feeding means fewer flowers.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: first-open date and any harvest cuts taken.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it bloomed and when you cut flowers.

growth_stages.name: Cut back
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The post-bloom hard prune, the single most important care act of the year. After flowering fades, shear the whole plant back by about a third.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The big yearly trim, right after the flowers fade. This is the one job that matters most for keeping lavender alive and bushy.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Spent, browning flower spikes and a plant that has finished its main bloom. Below the green growth you will see bare woody stems; these are your no-cut zone.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Faded, brownish flowers and a plant that is done blooming. Notice the hard woody stems below the green; never cut into those.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Shear the plant back by about a third, cutting into soft green growth only and never into the bare woody base, which will not resprout. Time it after flowering rather than in midsummer, when a cut removes the season's blooms in progress.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim about a third off the plant, cutting only into the soft green parts, never down into the hard woody stems, because those will not grow back. Do it after it finishes flowering, not in the middle of summer.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Cut back: date sheared and roughly how much removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you did the big trim.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (cold zones)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, lavender goes dormant. It needs almost no water, and it is wet soil or a late fall cut, not the cold itself, that usually kills it over winter.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Where winters freeze, lavender rests through the cold months. It barely needs water, and it is soggy soil or a late-season trim, not the cold, that usually kills it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A plant that has stopped growing for the season. English lavender holds much of its gray foliage; tender Spanish and French types decline in cold and need protection or to come indoors.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A plant that has stopped growing. The hardy English kind keeps much of its gray leaves; the tender frilly types fade in the cold and need shelter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop watering and feeding, and leave any hard pruning for spring. Protect tender types or move container plants under cover. In zone 4, mulch or a sheltered south-facing spot helps English lavender overwinter.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Stop watering and feeding, and save any big trim for spring. Shelter the tender types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. In very cold areas, a sheltered spot or mulch helps the hardy kind survive.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Dormancy: date growth stopped and any winter protection applied.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it went dormant and any winter cover you added.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your plant-out window is open. Set the nursery plant in full sun in sharply drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart. Skip rich compost and fertilizer.
notifications.body_beginner: It is time to plant your lavender. Put it in a sunny, well-draining spot now that frost has passed, leaving 18 to 24 inches between plants, and do not add fertilizer.

notifications.body_seasoned: Blooms are fading, time to shear it back by a third, staying above the woody base. Cut into soft green growth only; the bare wood below will not resprout. This yearly cut keeps the plant compact and long-lived.
notifications.body_beginner: Your lavender flowers are fading, so trim about a third off, cutting only into the soft green growth and staying above the hard woody stems, which will not grow back. This yearly trim keeps it bushy.

notifications.title_beginner: Get your lavender ready for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: Cold is coming. Stop watering and feeding, leave any hard pruning for spring, and protect tender Spanish or French types or move container plants under cover. Wet winter soil, not cold, is the usual killer.
notifications.body_beginner: Winter is coming. Stop watering and feeding, save any big trim for spring, and shelter the tender frilly types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills lavender.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost on tender new growth
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Late frost on the new growth
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A late spring frost is forecast while the plant is pushing tender new growth. Hold off on any planned hard pruning until frost has fully passed, and protect newly set-out plants overnight.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A late spring frost is coming while your lavender has soft new growth. Wait to do any big trimming until frost is fully over, and cover any just-planted lavender overnight.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, humid weather raises rot risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A spell of humid heat is forecast, which raises the risk of root rot and leaf spot in muggy regions. Do not add water on lavender's account, make sure it is not sitting wet, and keep airflow open around the plant.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, sticky weather is coming, which can lead to rot and leaf spots. Do not give lavender extra water, make sure it is not sitting in wet soil, and keep the area around it open and airy.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Wet winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Soggy winter soil is the real risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Prolonged wet soil is forecast heading into or during winter dormancy. Wet winter ground, not cold, is what usually kills lavender, so make sure it is not sitting in water and consider moving containers under cover.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A long wet spell is coming around winter. Soggy soil, not the cold, is what usually kills lavender, so make sure it is not standing in water, and move pots somewhere protected if you can.

transplant.text_seasoned: Plant lavender lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine other plants want, set it in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed rather than digging in sand. Rich, wet soil is what kills lavender.
transplant.text_beginner: Lavender does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy clay, plant it on a little mound or raised bed so water drains away.

transplant.text_seasoned: Space plants 18 to 24 inches apart and give each one room to breathe. Good air circulation between plants is one of the simplest ways to head off the fungal problems lavender is prone to in damp conditions.
transplant.text_beginner: Leave about 18 to 24 inches between plants. That space lets air move around each one, which helps prevent the fungal problems lavender can get when it stays damp.

establishment.text_seasoned: Year one is about roots, not flowers. Water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper toward deep and infrequent. Pinch the first flowers and lightly shape the plant so it builds out bushy; it will reach full size in about three years and live well over a decade.
establishment.text_beginner: The first year is about growing roots, not flowers. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Pinch off the first few flowers and lightly shape it so it grows bushy. It takes about three years to reach full size.

establishment.text_seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Lavender has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft leafy growth at the expense of flowers. The same goes for water: more is not better.
establishment.text_beginner: Try not to feed it. Lavender needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives you lots of leaves but fewer flowers. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Watch for fresh green growth low on the plant each spring; that is your signal it came through winter. As the soil warms, settle into deep but infrequent watering rather than frequent shallow sips.
vegetative.text_beginner: In spring, look for new green growth low on the plant. That means it survived winter. As the weather warms, water deeply but not very often instead of a little bit every day.

vegetative.text_seasoned: If you saved a hard prune for spring, make it once green growth has emerged and frost has passed, around early in the season. Cut into green growth only; the bare woody stems below will not resprout.
vegetative.text_beginner: If you waited until spring to do the big trim, do it once you see green growth and frost is over. Cut only into the green parts, because the hard woody stems below will not grow back.

bloom.text_seasoned: For the best fragrance and dried color, cut flower stems as the lowest flowers on each spike begin to open, rather than waiting for full bloom. Harvest in the morning once the dew has dried.
bloom.text_beginner: For the best scent and color, cut the flower stems when the bottom flowers on each spike are just starting to open, not when fully bloomed. Cut in the morning after the dew dries.

bloom.text_seasoned: To dry lavender, gather small bundles and hang them upside down somewhere warm, dark, and airy, then store the dried flowers sealed. For cooking, use only your own unsprayed lavender, never florist or nursery stock, and English types most of all.
bloom.text_beginner: To dry it, tie small bunches and hang them upside down somewhere warm and airy, then store the dried flowers in a sealed jar. If you want to cook with it, use only your own lavender that has not been sprayed, and the English kind works best.

cut_back.text_seasoned: This is the cut that keeps lavender alive. After bloom fades, shear the whole plant back by about a third, cutting into soft green growth only and never into the bare woody base, which will not resprout. Skip this yearly cut and the plant turns leggy, splits open at the center, and declines within a few years.
cut_back.text_beginner: This trim is what keeps lavender going. After it finishes flowering, cut about a third off the plant, going only into the soft green growth and never down into the hard woody stems, because those will not grow back. Skip it year after year and the plant gets tall and woody, flops open in the middle, and slowly dies.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Time the cut after flowering, not in midsummer. A July prune removes the season's blooms while they are still developing, so wait until the main flush has faded before you shear.
cut_back.text_beginner: Do the big trim after it flowers, not in the middle of summer. Trimming in July cuts off flowers that are still forming, so wait until the main bloom has faded.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave any hard pruning for spring. A dormant plant in wet soil rots, and a fresh fall cut leaves it vulnerable, so the worst things you can do are water it and prune it late.
dormancy.text_beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the big trim for spring. A resting plant sitting in wet soil rots, and a late trim leaves it weak, so do not water it or cut it back now.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Protect the tender types. Spanish and French lavenders are not cold hardy and are best grown in containers brought under cover for winter, while English lavender overwinters outdoors through about zone 5, or zone 4 with good drainage and a sheltered, mulched spot.
dormancy.text_beginner: Shelter the tender kinds. Spanish and French lavender are not cold hardy, so grow them in pots you can bring somewhere protected for winter. English lavender can stay outside through cold winters if it has good drainage and a sheltered spot.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature plant yields many cuttable flower spikes each summer (often dozens of stems), enough for fresh bouquets plus bundles for drying; productivity peaks once the plant reaches full size at about three years.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown lavender gives you plenty of flower stems each summer, enough to cut for the house and to dry, especially once it is a few years old.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect little to no usable harvest the first year; pinching early flowers to build a bushy framework pays off in later seasons.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect much the first year. Trimming off the first flowers helps the plant bulk up for bigger harvests later.
factors_seasoned: Plant age and size (full production at about three years)
Species and cultivar (lavandins yield more, larger stems than English types)
Full sun and lean, sharply drained soil
Annual hard cut-back to keep the plant productive and non-woody

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves turning yellow or the plant dying back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: With lavender, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering and poor drainage are the number one killer, leading to root and crown rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: For lavender, yellow leaves and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering and soggy soil are the biggest killer. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and on clay use a mound or raised bed. Never let lavender sit in wet ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but only once in a while, and on heavy soil plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tall and woody with a gap in the middle
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A plant that has gone leggy and woody and flopped open at the center missed its annual cut-back. Without the yearly post-bloom prune, lavender stops renewing its compact form and declines within a few years.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: When lavender gets tall and woody and splits open in the middle, it missed its yearly trim. Without that trim after flowering, it stops staying bushy and slowly falls apart.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Shear by about a third every year after bloom, cutting into green growth only and never into the bare wood, which will not resprout. A badly overgrown plant often cannot be fully renovated and may be better replaced.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Trim about a third off every year after it flowers, cutting only into the green and never into the hard wood, which will not grow back. A plant that is already very woody often cannot be saved and may be worth replacing.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sparse flowering usually means too much feed or too much shade. Over-fertilizing drives soft leafy growth at the expense of blooms, and lavender needs full sun to flower well.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Few flowers usually means too much fertilizer or too much shade. Feeding it too much gives leaves instead of flowers, and lavender needs full sun to bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Stop fertilizing and make sure the plant gets full sun. Lavender has low fertility needs, and lean, dry, sunny conditions produce the most flowers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Stop feeding it and make sure it gets full sun. Lavender needs very little, and poor, dry, sunny conditions give you the most flowers.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lavender is edible in small culinary amounts for people but is a low-severity toxin in quantity, and it is a hazard to cats, dogs, and horses, which can react to its compounds (linalool and linalyl acetate). This is worth knowing, not a reason to avoid growing it.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Lavender is fine for people in small amounts in cooking, but eating a lot is mildly toxic, and it can make cats, dogs, and horses sick. Good to know, not a reason to skip it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep pets from grazing on lavender, and use only your own unsprayed plants, never florist or nursery stock, for any culinary use. If a pet eats a large amount, contact your veterinarian.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep pets from eating the plant, and only cook with your own lavender that has not been sprayed. If a pet eats a lot, call your vet.

succession_policy.tip_beginner: N/A. You plant lavender once; you do not resow it through the season.

open_findings.summary: UAEX DOES publish a hardiness range for Lavandula angustifolia, and it differs from ours. Its English Lavender Plant of the Week (Gerald Klingaman, 2007-07-20) states "Lavender is hardy from zones 5 to 8"; our prose carries "zones 5a to 9b", which is NC State's Toolbox value and matches lavender.hardiness_zone_max = 9. The false UAEX credit was removed 2026-07-31 and the NC State number retained unattributed. IF mid_south lavender is ever repointed to the real UAEX Plant of the Week URL (the one genuine repoint this hunt found, and the fix for its bare host), the z8 cell MUST change with it: it reads "zone 8 sits comfortably inside English lavender's zone 5 to 9b hardy range", and under UAEX's number zone 8 is the CEILING, not comfortably inside. Note also that the UAEX page supports the root-rot/humidity framing but never mentions leaf spot.

The warm_arid zone 8 cell publishes plant_out "Apr - May or Sep - Oct" and cites three NMSU sources. NONE of them publishes a lavender planting date. NMSU Guide H-221 "Spices and Herbs for the Home Garden" gives lavender seed-germination guidance only (moist refrigerated storage for three days; 30 days to germinate at 65 degrees F or higher) and no planting month or season. NMSU RR-770 is "Lavender Cultivar Trial Results for North-Central New Mexico, 2003 through 2005", a research report whose only date is when the trial plot was established (June 24, 2002) and whose geography is north-central New Mexico, not the southern warm_arid band this cell describes. The NMSU low-water-plants herbaceous list covers the right taxon (Lavandula angustifolia) and gives water need, mature height and sun exposure, but states no planting time and no hardiness zone. So the window is modeled and says so nowhere. TWO CITATIONS ARE ALSO MISLABELLED, which is how this stayed invisible: the low-water list is cited under nmsu_chart, whose catalog entry is the Dona Ana Food Garden Planting Chart, and RR-770 is cited under nmsu_donaana_mg, whose catalog entry is the Dona Ana Master Gardeners site. plantings.label: establishment
plantings.synthesis_note_seasoned: Region-constant arms span the northern tier's zone range. Plant-out runs from the warmest zone's last spring frost (zone 7, mid-March) to the coldest zone's (zone 3, late May); lavender is set out as a nursery transplant after the last spring frost (USU). The bloom arm spans the per-zone early-summer windows, earliest in zone 7 and latest in zone 3. Bloom is frost-resolved from the T1 early-summer flowering phenology (UC Marin Master Gardeners: blooms late spring into summer; RHS: flowers in summer), not read from a planting-date table; the per-zone display windows are computed from each zone's last spring frost.
plantings.synthesis_note_beginner: These cover the whole northern tier. Set lavender out after your last spring frost, which falls anywhere from mid-March in the mildest spots to late May in the coldest. It flowers in early summer, a little sooner in the warmer zones and a little later in the coldest ones.

plantings_provenance.note: plant_out + bloom arms are frost-resolved off zone_frost_data (last_spring) per zone, then spanned across the region. Bloom phenology anchor: early-summer flowering (UC MG county pages under UC ANR; RHS). A5: phenology relationship anchored, calendar months resolved per zone, never analogized from a warmer region's literal month read.

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Annual or container. Zone 3 is well below English lavender's hardy range, so it is grown as a single-season plant or as a container plant brought in for winter. With a short frost-free season (about 120 days), set nursery transplants out promptly after the last spring frost to get a first-summer bloom before the first fall frost ends the season.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Lavender cannot survive a zone 3 winter outdoors, so grow it for the season or in a pot you bring inside. Summers are short here, so plant it as soon as your last spring frost has passed to enjoy the blooms before fall frost.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too cold to overwinter reliably in the ground here, so grow lavender as an annual or in a container you move under cover for winter. Set plants out only after the last spring frost; the season ends at the first fall frost.

description_seasoned: Lavender is a woody Mediterranean perennial sub-shrub in the mint family, grown for its fragrant summer flower spikes and silvery, aromatic foliage. It thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, and its defining care act is an annual hard cut-back after bloom that keeps it compact and prevents it from going woody and splitting open. English lavender is both the hardiest type and the one used in cooking, while the showy Spanish and French types are tender and ornamental.
description_beginner: Lavender is a small woody shrub with silvery leaves and fragrant purple flower spikes in summer. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. The one job that matters is trimming it back every year after it flowers so it stays bushy instead of turning into bare woody sticks. English lavender is the hardy, cook-with-it kind; the frillier Spanish and French types are mainly for looks and are not cold-hardy.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut for fresh bouquets when about half the buds on a spike have opened; cut for drying or culinary use a little earlier, when only the first one or two buds on the spike have opened, so the buds hold their color and oils. Harvest in the morning after the dew dries but before the heat, when the fragrance is most concentrated.
harvest_ready_beginner: For a fresh vase, cut the stems when about half the little buds on the spike have opened. For drying or cooking, cut a bit sooner, when just the first couple of buds have opened. Cut in the morning once the dew has dried, when lavender smells strongest.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is the hardiest type, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9 and surviving zone 4 with good drainage and winter protection. Lavandins are nearly as hardy. Spanish and French lavenders are tender (about zone 7 to 8 and warmer) and are grown as container plants brought in for winter in colder regions. Good drainage matters as much as cold: lavender rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it.
hardiness_notes_beginner: English lavender is the toughest and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 if you protect it). The showy Spanish and French types are not cold-hardy, so in cold areas grow them in pots you bring inside for winter. Just as important as cold: lavender hates wet feet in winter and will rot in soggy soil.
year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on root establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper off. Pinch or lightly clip flowers and shape the young plant to encourage bushy lateral growth rather than letting it flower heavily; it will reach full size in about three years and live well over a decade with the right lean, dry conditions.
year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the roots going. Water it fairly regularly until it is established, then cut back. It helps to trim it lightly and not let it flower too hard the first season, so it grows bushy. It takes about three years to reach full size and can live for more than ten.
soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Work an inch of coarse compost into the top several inches of soil, and on heavy clay improve drainage with a raised bed or mound rather than by digging in sand, which can worsen drainage in clay. Aim for lean, gritty, near-neutral to slightly alkaline ground.
soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. Mix a little coarse compost into the top of the soil. If your ground is heavy clay, plant lavender in a raised bed or mound instead, because that drains better. The goal is poor, gritty soil, not rich soil.
bloom_time_beginner: Lavender flowers in summer. Some kinds (English types) bloom in early summer and may flower again later; the big hybrid types bloom once, a little later. When yours blooms depends on where you live.
bloom_time_seasoned: Lavender blooms in summer; English types often flower in late spring to early summer and may rebloom later in the season, while lavandins bloom once, later in summer. Exact timing shifts with your region and is set per zone.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: In zones with freezing winters, lavender goes dormant. Hold off on watering and feeding, leave any hard pruning for spring, and protect tender Spanish or French types or move container plants under cover. A dormant plant needs almost no water, and it is wet soil or a fresh fall cut, not the cold itself, that usually rots or kills it over winter.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Where winters freeze, lavender rests through the cold months. Stop watering and feeding it, save any big trim for spring, and in cold areas shelter the tender types or bring potted plants somewhere protected. A resting plant barely needs water, and it is usually soggy soil or a late-season haircut, not the cold, that kills lavender over winter.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Lavender is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner; it is grown for its flowers, not fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its blooms are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one lavender plant for it to flower well; it does not need a partner plant. Bees love the flowers, but that is a bonus for your garden, not something the plant needs to bloom.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: After the flowers fade, shear the whole plant back by about a third, cutting into soft green growth only and never into the bare woody base, which will not resprout. This yearly cut is what keeps lavender compact and long-lived; without it the plant turns leggy, splits open at the center, and declines within a few years.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Once it finishes flowering, trim about a third off the plant, cutting only into the soft green parts and never down into the hard, woody stems, because those will not grow back. Do this every year and your lavender stays round and bushy. Skip it and the plant gets tall and woody, flops open in the middle, and slowly dies off.

pet_safe.note: Its essential oils (linalool) can cause mild stomach upset in cats, dogs, and horses if eaten.
